204: \paragraph{How tight are the endpoint certificates on recorded states?}
205: The relative-weight construction in \Cref{cor:tanh-relative-weights} permits
206: uniform and category-specific endpoint comparisons without using the Hessian
207: path envelope.  A feature category groups observations with the same fixed
208: context--action feature vector.  In this model, parameter updates change the
209: scalar gradient coefficient in that feature direction.  The category
210: construction compares the accumulated squared coefficients at collection
211: time with those obtained at the current parameter.
212: 
213: After observing the outcomes, we audit these comparisons on
214: the same 600 recorded histories, replaying representation updates with the
215: recorded actions and rewards.  On Hessian's histories, the category-specific
216: outward factor gives mean
217: effective-width overheads of $0.28\%$--$12.68\%$ relative to the direct reference
218: width, versus $0.16\%$--$12.13\%$ for the dense endpoint factor across conditions
219: (\Cref{app:transport-followup}).  These are means of actionwise ratios, not
220: ratios of mean widths: for each candidate action at each recorded state, we
221: divide its effective width by its reference width, then average over actions,
222: rounds, and seeds.
223: 
224: This calculation shows the size of the certificate overhead on existing
225: states.  It evaluates neither a new adaptive policy nor end-to-end speed.
226: The relative certificate bounds the endpoint comparison, not the length of
227: the original interpolated factor path, and leaves the historical and current
228: approximation-error charges in place.  As \Cref{prop:reference-width-floor}
229: explains, tightening the certificate creates no additional statistical
230: information and does not order policies' adaptive regret.
